andreeva-wta-finals.headline: Teenager Mirra Andreeva wins WTA Finals title
andreeva-wta-finals.body_md:
Mirra Andreeva has won the WTA Finals, beating Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 in Sunday's final at Indian Wells to take the season-ending championship on her first appearance. She is 19. She did not drop a set all week.

The result also corrects the tidy assumption that the tour's showpiece wrapped up early this month. It finished on 15 November, and the champion was worth the wait.

## The final

It was closer than the scoreline suggests. Andreeva served for the first set at 5-4, then hit two double faults and a long backhand to let Svitolina back in. She broke in the next game and held on to take the set after 55 minutes.

The second turned on a 10-minute seventh game, the longest of the tournament, which went to six deuces before Svitolina held for 4-3. It was the last thing she won comfortably. Andreeva held easily, broke for the sixth time in the match and closed it out when Svitolina put an overhead into the net on match point. The whole thing took one hour and 48 minutes.

Afterwards Andreeva credited her team, led by coach Conchita Martinez. "I'm super thankful to my team for helping me work hard every day and pushing me to my limits," she said.

Svitolina, 32, the 2018 champion, is back at this level after pregnancy. "Hopefully it inspires some ladies and athletes around the world to believe that it's possible," she said. She did not shake hands at the net, consistent with her long-standing stance on Russian and Belarusian opponents.

## The week

Andreeva's route was clean. She beat Svitolina 6-4, 6-0 in the round-robin stage, then Aryna Sabalenka, and later got past Jessica Pegula in the semi-final to set up the rematch. Five matches, five wins, no sets lost: reports describe her as the first player to win the title on debut while unbeaten throughout.

The reward was the maximum $3.37m in prize money, the Billie Jean King Trophy and, from the sponsor, a custom Mercedes-Benz AMG SL 55 in the WTA's purple. She does not yet have a driving licence.

She is the youngest champion at the event since Maria Sharapova in 2004. The title is her fourth of 2026 and her seventh overall, and it lifts her to a career-high world No. 2 in Monday's rankings, within 300 points of Elena Rybakina at the top.

## A displaced event

The tournament was staged in California only because it was moved from Riyadh, which was changed because of the US-Israeli war on Iran. It goes to Charlotte, North Carolina, next year. Andreeva will be among those arriving with a target on her back.

In doubles, Katerina Siniakova and Taylor Townsend beat Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini in the final.

The next test is the new season's opening Grand Slam in Melbourne in January, where Andreeva will be one of the players to beat. A rankings gap that small at the top will not stay closed for long.

england-beat-spain-tuchel.headline: England beat Spain in a tense Tuchel-era win
england-beat-spain-tuchel.body_md:
England did not beat Spain. Not in the match that can be verified, anyway. The most recent meeting of the two sides that could be found was won by Spain, 3-2, at Wembley on 26 September, in the UEFA Nations League. A report that England beat Spain in a tense Thomas Tuchel-era win could not be matched to any fixture, and no scoreline, scorers or competition were available to check it against.

## What the record shows

The September match was a five-goal game, and England were the ones who let it slip. Reports of the night describe a side that held a second-half lead and then gave it away through defensive errors. Spain's first two goals followed two sloppy mistakes at the back. Anthony Gordon equalised for England, and Mikel Oyarzabal tucked away the winner after a through pass from Baena.

One report noted it was the first time since June 2019 that England had made two errors leading to goals in a competitive match.

That sits badly with the line in the brief that England led for 60 minutes of near-perfect play. A long lead, a late collapse and a Spanish rally fit the September match as described. A win does not fit it.

## Tuchel's verdict

Tuchel, England's head coach since January 2025, did not dress the defeat up. He pointed to the number of "clear-cut mistakes" and insisted England could still beat the best sides. He noted that at the World Cup they had beaten three top-ten teams. His line, in the words of one report, was that England would "keep on pushing" to reach Spain's level.

That is the useful frame for any England–Spain story this year. Spain are the benchmark Tuchel keeps measuring his side against, and the September result left the gap in view.

## What would change this

If England and Spain have met again since September, in a friendly or elsewhere, a win would be a real story: the first over this Spain side under Tuchel. That would need a confirmed date, venue, scoreline and scorers from BBC Sport or the Football Association before it could run as written. None of those was found.

Until then, the checkable result stands: Spain 3, England 2, with Tuchel's side left to explain two errors and a lead that did not last.

scotland-australia-arm-wrestle.headline: Scotland's defence holds in an 'arm wrestle' against Australia
scotland-australia-arm-wrestle.body_md:
Scotland beat Australia 15-12 at Murrayfield in a Nations Championship fixture that never loosened its grip, and their head coach, Gregor Townsend, said afterwards that the defence was the reason. The win came a week after a loss to New Zealand and lifted Scotland back above Wales into fourth place in the Northern Hemisphere table.

## A match decided by tackles

The game was low on fluency and high on contact. Scotland led 12-5 at half-time after tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey, then spent much of the second half absorbing Australian pressure rather than adding to the total. Finn Russell's late penalty stretched the margin from five points to eight, and Townsend defended the choice to kick for the posts rather than chase a third try.

> "I think the right decision was to go for the three points to get more than a score ahead."

The call mattered. Australia's Max Jorgensen scored in the 80th minute, following Harry Potter's earlier try, and the final gap was three points rather than the one it would have been without Russell's kick. Australia's 12 points were their lowest return since a 25-7 loss to England in November 2025.

Townsend was unusually emphatic about the defensive work.

> "I think that's one of our best defensive performances over the last few years," he said. "The shots going in in the first half and the effort that went into the second half was outstanding."

He added that Scotland "deserved the win given the effort that went in and the fact we led throughout the game." It was Scotland's fifth win in six meetings with Australia.

## Absences and what comes next

Scotland managed it without their captain. Sione Tuipulotu was ruled out before kick-off with a knee injury, and lock Scott Cummings left in the first half with a thigh problem. Townsend said an ultrasound scan looked encouraging but that an MRI is likely, and he described Cummings as a doubt for next week.

That matters because the table is tight and the margin for error is small. Scotland missed a bonus point against Australia, which limits how far they can climb, and Townsend said a bonus-point win would be needed to go higher. Japan are the next opponents, and the fitness of Cummings and Tuipulotu will shape the team Townsend names for that game.

mcilroy-record-win.headline: Tearful McIlroy dedicates record-equalling win to ill father
mcilroy-record-win.body_md:
Rory McIlroy fought back tears in Dubai on Sunday as he secured a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title and dedicated it to his father, Gerry, who is still recovering in hospital after a double lung transplant.

McIlroy did not win the tournament itself. Tyrrell Hatton took the DP World Tour Championship at Jumeirah Golf Estates. McIlroy finished solo second on 10 under par, after a closing 67. That was enough to win the season-long money list. It also drew him level with Colin Montgomerie, who won the order of merit eight times.

## The record

McIlroy finished one place ahead of Eugenio Chacarra, who led the standings going into the final event and ended two strokes behind him, tied for third. The title is McIlroy's fifth in a row. Alongside Montgomerie, he now shares the most in the history of the European circuit, which is now branded the DP World Tour.

The record is significant in its own right, though it is a season-long prize rather than a single tournament. It rewards consistency over a whole year, which is the quality Montgomerie was known for in the 1990s. McIlroy has said the title "felt different" from his recent wins, and that he had to work hard for it.

> "Very proud to win this again, and yeah, put my name alongside Monty's with eight."

## The dedication

The emotion came from what McIlroy said about his father. Gerry McIlroy had a double lung transplant in September. He has spent about two months in hospital, including many days in intensive care. McIlroy said the operation was a success and that his father is recovering steadily.

Before McIlroy left for the Middle East, Gerry gave him an instruction: "win me The Race to Dubai." McIlroy said that stayed with him through the week. Reports quoted him saying, with his voice breaking, "This one is for him."

> "My dad — hopefully everyone's dad in this room — is a massive part of my life, and has been my biggest supporter."

Gerry has been a fixture of McIlroy's career since the beginning. He worked extra jobs to fund his son's early golf. McIlroy has paid tribute to both parents after his biggest wins, including his second Masters in April.

## What comes next

The immediate question is Gerry's recovery. McIlroy's season is over, and he can go home to his father. On the course, a ninth Race to Dubai title would put him alone at the top. The 2027 season is the next chance to win it.

*Details here are drawn from ESPN and Yahoo Sports reports of the final round. Some accounts differ slightly on the length of Gerry McIlroy's hospital stay.*

korea-tax-exam-cheating.headline: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
korea-tax-exam-cheating.body_md:
South Korea's top scorer on this year's tax accountancy exam has admitted to cheating. By his own account, he used a miniature camera, a smartphone and generative AI to answer the questions. Having first denied any wrongdoing, he made the confession in a video posted to his lawyer's YouTube channel. Police have opened an investigation.

The case is a long way from the market stories elsewhere in this edition. It matters mainly to the exam authorities and to the accountancy profession in Korea.

## A score too good to ignore

What drew attention was the result. Reports say he answered 159 of the 160 questions correctly in the first-stage exam in April, for 397.5 out of 400. He then scored 663 out of 800 in the second-stage written paper and was named overall top scorer. The marks drew public scrutiny, and he denied cheating at first. Some Korean outlets also reported that the administering body, the Human Resources Development Service of Korea, had said it found nothing unusual.

His confession has since reversed that. He said he photographed the exam questions with a micro-camera, passed them to an AI tool and read the answers off a phone. Korean outlets report that he said he used the same method on the first-stage exam for certified public accountants. That claim has not been tested and sits with the investigators.

## What happens next

The response has been quick. Police have assigned the case to a public-crime investigation unit. The government has said it is considering a criminal complaint and suspending the validity of his pass. Under the penalty the government has set for confirmed AI cheating in this exam, the qualification would be revoked and the person barred from the exam for five years.

Legal commentators quoted in the Korean press suggest a court might impose a custodial sentence to deter others. They also note that his voluntary admission and cooperation could count in his favour.

The authorities say they are working on tighter controls against AI-enabled devices in exam halls. The scandal also lands about a week before the national college entrance exam. In a country where standardised tests largely shape careers and social mobility, a credential is only useful if the public trusts the score behind it.

## The wider question

The unresolved issue is how far the method reaches. If the confession about the accountants' exam holds up, the damage goes beyond one licence. Details still differ between outlets, and the BBC report was available only through secondary summaries. The next marker is the police inquiry and the formal decision on his qualification.

wealthy-americans-retirement-gap.headline: Wealthy Americans haven't saved enough for retirement either
wealthy-americans-retirement-gap.body_md:
A retirement shortfall is usually pictured as a problem of the low-paid: people on thin wages, with patchy pension coverage and little left over at the end of the month. A newly released survey from HSBC suggests the gap reaches a good deal further up the income ladder. Americans who count as affluent say they have so far put aside roughly half of what they think they will need.

The research, conducted by Ipsos and reported by Fortune on 3 November, defines affluent as having at least $100,000 in investable assets. Those respondents put the sum needed for a comfortable retirement at $2.6m, up 26% on a year earlier. On average they have saved 52% of it. The sample size and the survey's formal name were not given in the coverage, and the full methodology has not been checked here.

## A target that keeps moving

The arithmetic is partly about the goalposts. A 26% rise in the stated target in twelve months means that even steady saving can leave someone further from the line than before. The figures vary sharply by age:

- Baby boomers: 74% of their goal
- Gen X: 55%
- Gen Z: 45%
- Millennials: 42%

No generation is fully on track, and the cohorts furthest from retirement are the ones with the most ground to cover. That is a smaller worry than it sounds for Gen Z, who have decades of contributions ahead. For millennials, who are mid-career and often carrying housing and childcare costs, it is harder to wave away.

"A comfortable retirement is becoming more expensive, even for those who have substantial wealth," said Racquel Oden, HSBC's US head of international wealth and premier banking.

## Longer lives, longer lists

The survey suggests the money is being asked to do more than it once did. Some 43% of respondents named funding retirement as their top goal, but 37% also cited supporting children and ageing parents, and 39% personal or professional reinvention. Longevity is changing the plan: 59% said living longer has altered their legacy intentions, and 31% are putting more towards their own future costs even if that shrinks what heirs receive. Almost half (48%) said their main aim is for children or grandchildren to become fully financially independent.

Health care sits underneath much of this. Fidelity's July estimate is that a 65-year-old retiring this year can expect to spend an average of $185,500 on health care, up 7.5% year on year, a figure that does not care much about the size of the portfolio around it.

Other surveys point the same way, though they are not directly comparable. BlackRock found respondents saying they need about $2.1m, with 62% holding less than $150,000. Catherine Collinson, chief executive of the Transamerica Institute, described the combination of pressures as "a perfect storm".

## What it means for the usual advice

Self-reported targets are not the same as actuarial need, and a survey of people with $100,000 or more in assets is a wide net; it takes in many who would not think of themselves as wealthy. Respondents may also name a number that reflects anxiety as much as arithmetic. Similar findings go back more than a decade, when Natixis found that many millionaires did not know how much they needed.

Still, the pattern challenges a comfortable assumption. If households with real assets and decent incomes also feel short, then "save more" is incomplete advice. The harder questions are what retirement is expected to pay for, how long it must last, and how much of the bill falls on children and parents at the same time. The next data point to watch is whether the stated target keeps climbing when HSBC repeats the research next year.

black-friday-tax-scams.headline: Black Friday and tax return scams: how to spot them
black-friday-tax-scams.body_md:
Every autumn the same email arrives, dressed a little differently. A parcel could not be delivered. A tax refund is waiting. A games console is on sale at a price that no retailer could sustain. With Black Friday falling on Friday 27 November, the day after US Thanksgiving, the season when shoppers are most distracted and most willing to click is nearly here.

This is a reminder rather than a scoop. The BBC's latest consumer-advice item, which prompted this note, gives no new loss figures, victim counts or novel scam methods, and none are claimed here. Nothing in it points to an effect on markets. What it offers is a seasonal checklist, and the checklist is worth repeating because the tricks hardly change.

## The shop that is too good to be true

The classic Black Friday fraud is the fake storefront: a slick website, often built in an afternoon, advertising branded goods at deep discounts. The buyer pays by card or bank transfer and receives nothing, or a counterfeit. Social-media adverts and sponsored search results carry many of them, because a convincing logo costs almost nothing to copy.

The usual defences are unglamorous:

- Check the web address closely. Lookalike domains with an extra word or a swapped letter are common.
- Be wary of any price far below every other retailer's. Real sales trim margins; they do not abolish them.
- Pay by credit card where possible. In the UK, Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act makes the card issuer jointly liable for purchases between £100 and £30,000, a protection that bank transfers lack.
- Avoid sellers who insist on transfers, gift cards or cryptocurrency.

## Delivery texts and the tax refund

Black Friday also fills inboxes with parcels, which makes fake delivery notices plausible. A text claiming a package is held and asking for a small redelivery fee is designed to harvest card details, not to move a box. The safer route is to go to the retailer's or courier's own app or website rather than follow a link.

Tax-return scams ride a different calendar but the same psychology. In the UK, the Self Assessment deadline on 31 January draws a steady flow of messages impersonating HMRC, offering a refund or threatening penalties and asking for bank details. Tax authorities in both Britain and the US say they do not demand payment or personal data by text or unsolicited email, and that genuine refunds are not arranged through links in messages. Urgency is the tell: a deadline of hours, a threat of arrest, a refund that must be claimed now.

## What to do if caught out

The advice is consistent across regulators and banks. Contact the card issuer or bank at once, using the number on the card rather than one in the message. Change passwords on any account that shared the compromised details. Report the attempt: in the UK, suspicious emails go to the National Cyber Security Centre and texts can be forwarded to 7726, while Action Fraud takes reports of losses. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission runs ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

The next fixed dates are plain enough. Black Friday itself arrives on 27 November, with Cyber Monday following on 30 November, and the Self Assessment deadline lands at the end of January. Fraud reports tend to be tallied afterwards, and any figures showing whether the problem is growing will come from those releases, not from the advice that precedes them.
black-friday-tax-scams.in_one_sentence: With Black Friday on 27 November, consumer advice repeats familiar warnings on fake shops, delivery texts and tax-refund phishing; no new loss data or scam types are reported.

gta6-secrecy.headline: Even GTA's original creators haven't played GTA 6
gta6-secrecy.body_md:
Grand Theft Auto VI goes on sale on 19 November, three days from now. Players who have queued for years will be among the first to see it. The people who started the series are not.

Rockstar Games has run one of the tightest launch campaigns in the industry. The studio has released two trailers and a small number of screenshots, and little else. Even the people closest to the franchise's history are watching from outside.

Dan Houser, the Rockstar co-founder who wrote the modern GTA games, has said he has not watched the GTA VI reveal and plans to keep it that way. "I will try and avoid it because I always try and avoid stuff that's going to distract or disrupt me creatively," he said, as reported by Games.gg. He has also said he wrote none of the new game: the world, he told PC Gamer, has "probably had enough GTA from me".

Houser is a Rockstar founder, though, not one of the original 1997 team. That game was made in Dundee by DMA Design, the studio David Jones founded in 1987, and the lineage matters to the story. Jones and the early developers have said little publicly about GTA VI, and nothing found in reporting for this piece shows whether any of them has seen more than the public trailers. The headline's claim is best read as the broad point: the secrecy extends far beyond the gaming press.

## A studio that grew from a handful of people

DMA Design became Rockstar North. By 2018 it employed around 650 people, a long way from the small Scottish team that shipped the first game. The relationship has not always been warm. Jones has said Rockstar filed copyright claims against videos he posted showing prototype builds of the original game, a reminder that the company guards even its oldest material.

The delay history reinforces the pattern. Rockstar first targeted May 2026, then announced in November 2025 that the game would slip to 19 November 2026. Take-Two has since said the date holds.

## Where the money is

The market link is more direct than the anecdote. Take-Two, Rockstar's publisher and parent, has built its financial year around this launch. Its most recent guidance, as reported, put fiscal 2027 net bookings at $8 billion to $8.2 billion, with adjusted earnings of $5.75 to $6 a share. That was below some analyst estimates, which ranged from about $8.5 billion to $9.1 billion depending on the source. Chief executive Strauss Zelnick has said preorders are running well ahead of expectations. The game is priced at $80.

Secrecy cuts both ways for investors. It sustains the anticipation that preorders feed on, and it leaves almost nothing for outsiders to check. Nobody beyond Rockstar can say how polished the game is, how large the day-one audience will be, or whether the guidance is cautious or merely hopeful. Shares have moved sharply on date announcements, which suggests the market treats each scrap of news as significant.

## What to watch

The first reviews and launch-week sales figures will test the guidance. Take-Two's next quarterly results, where the company is likely to update its full-year forecast, should show how much of the early demand has turned into bookings.
